Title: Why Cold Air or Hot Food Alone Can Trigger a Runny Nose

Description:
If cold air, dry indoor air, or a sudden weather change makes your nose run or clog up — even though allergy tests come back negative — you might be dealing with vasomotor rhinitis, not a typical allergy. The nasal lining overreacts to nonspecific triggers instead of a specific allergen: temperature swings, dry indoor air, and strong smells like perfume or smoke are the most common ones.

Buffer temperature swings with a scarf before you head outside, run a humidifier to keep indoor humidity between 40-60%, and use a saline nasal spray. Regular allergy pills often don't help here — azelastine and budesonide nasal sprays are approved specifically for nonallergic rhinitis, so ask your doctor about them if congestion sticks around for more than a few weeks.
